title: LPG and CNG Fuel System Safety
introduction: I start with the fuel type and the workshop conditions, because gas behavior matters before a tool touches the car. These precautions explain who may service LPG and CNG systems, where that work may happen and how liquid contact, accumulated gas and heat create hazards. They are safety requirements for specialist work, not instructions for tank removal or gas discharge.

edits.text: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) Fuel System Safety

WARNING: Only qualified personnel in authorized workshops may service Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) or Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) vehicle systems. Qualification requirements vary by region. Always comply with local laws and legislative directives governing CNG or LPG vehicle service. Failure to follow this instruction may result in serious personal injury or death.
edits.why: The required qualification and workshop authorization must be established before service begins; familiarity with conventional fuel systems does not satisfy this restriction.

edits.text: WARNING: Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) or Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) is highly flammable and toxic when contained in an unventilated work area. Work in a dedicated area with good ventilation and no ignition sources. Failure to follow these instructions may result in serious personal injury or death.
edits.why: Ventilation and ignition control address different hazards. Both conditions must be met in the designated work area.

edits.text: WARNING: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) can injure eyes and freeze skin. Always wear personal protective equipment, including safety goggles and gloves, to prevent contact with liquid gas. Failure to follow these instructions may result in serious personal injury.
edits.why: The contact hazard is with the liquid itself, so eye and hand protection remain necessary alongside ventilation.

edits.text: WARNING: Always comply with local regulations concerning storage or indoor parking of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) vehicles. Do not park these vehicles near heat sources, ignition sources or unventilated open pits. Failure to follow these instructions may result in serious personal injury.
edits.why: Storage requirements apply generally; the parking requirement specifically includes indoor parking. The prohibited parking locations must also be avoided.

edits.text: WARNING: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) is heavier than air and collects in low areas of buildings, including drains and work pits. Never discharge a tank inside a building. If possible, discharge the tank beforehand by running the vehicle. Any gas discharge must take place outdoors in a well-ventilated, flat area. Failure to follow these instructions may allow combustible gas to accumulate, causing personal injury or death in a fire or explosion.
edits.why: Low areas can collect gas even when the surrounding workspace appears open. The outdoor discharge requirement also applies when running the vehicle to use the fuel.

edits.text: WARNING: Extreme heat, including heat from paint drying ovens, increases Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) or Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) fuel tank pressure. Remove the fuel tank before using a paint drying oven at temperatures above 60° C. Failure to follow this instruction may release combustible gas, causing personal injury or death in a fire or explosion.
edits.why: Check the planned oven temperature before the vehicle enters the heating process. Tank removal requires the applicable specialist service instructions.

edits.text: WARNING: Improper handling of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) can harm your health. Always consult the LPG material safety information sheet before servicing an LPG vehicle. Failure to follow this instruction may result in serious personal injury or death.
edits.why: I make the LPG material safety information sheet an advance check so its health and handling precautions inform preparation before service begins. This requirement forms part of the precautions for qualified personnel working in authorized workshops.
